text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers.
- Trade Minister Johann Farnleitner threatens Austria's electricity industry with a state-run price policy, if firms try to raise household electricity prices once the market is liberalised.
- Due to the conflict between the USA and Iraq, oil prices are at their highest since the Gulf War. Austrian petrol prices are widely expected to rise in the next few days.

- Austria's Trade Minister Johann Farnleitner expects an outcome in the debate over longer shopping hours in Austria by November. Labour union spokesmen say they cannot see an early solution to the discussions
- Die Erste savings bank says it is no longer interested in buying the government's stake in Creditanstalt. Instead it plans to take over GiroCredit's offices abroad.
- Austrian ski maker Kaestle says it is moving two-thirds of its production to Slovenia, due to the continuing fall of prices of skis and snowboards.
- Austria's households save 400 schillings per month, says economic research institute Wifo. Last year the biggest drop was in food prices, this year it has been in industrial goods prices.
- The conservative People's Party says it will not accept a new call for bids for Creditanstalt. CA should either be sold to the consortium around EA-Generali or through the stock exchange, it says.
- Premium earnings of Insurer Wiener Staedtische have gone up 34 percent to 18.8 billion schillings in the first half of 1996.
- Finance Minister Viktor Klima says he must have some control over provincial budgets, so that Austria can make the criteria for the European Union's Monetary Union.
- The German unit of VA-Industrieanlagenbau Fuchs Systemtechnik has received an order to build a steel plant in China worth 300 million schillings.
- The European Union expects Austrian unemployment rates to rise to as much as 5.1 percent.
